0.title: The plug-in estimator falls below the true pass@k at every k >= 2; the combinatorial one sits exactly on it.
0.caption: Exact expectations (not simulation) over c ~ Binomial(16, 0.3) for one item with true p = 0.3 and n = 16 samples. The truth is 1-(1-p)^k. The unbiased curve is E[1 - C(n-c,k)/C(n,k)] and the plug-in curve is E[1-(1-c/n)^k], both computed with python3. The vertical line marks k = n/2, the largest k that `summarize` reports.

0.after: Running model code next to JAX
0.title: fork copies held locks and a live CUDA context; exec starts with nothing to inherit.
0.caption: Left: `fork` copies the whole address space but only the calling thread, so a lock an XLA thread held is copied in its locked state and nothing in the child can release it. Right: `verify_many` pool threads only wait on `subprocess.run`, and each child is a fresh `python -I -B` interpreter with rlimits and a minimal env.

0.title: A slow step 1 means step 0 returned a different cache key than it received.
0.caption: A schematic timeline, not measured durations. Top: the init state matches the step's outputs, so every step after the first hits the jit cache. Bottom: `jnp.asarray(0)` goes in weak-typed and comes out strong once the step combines it with a strong int32 (a plain `count + 1` would stay weak), so step 1 misses the cache and compiles again. After that the signature is stable.

1.after: Precision: why the masters are fp32 and the matmuls are not
1.title: In bf16, Adam's second moment cannot decay at all, and it stalls at 2.0 when the target is 4.
1.caption: This is a simulation, not a training run. The EMA $v \leftarrow 0.999\,v + 0.001\,g^2$ starts at v = 1 with a constant g², and every operation is rounded to the stated dtype (numpy with ml_dtypes bfloat16). In fp32, v relaxes toward g². In bf16, 0.999·v rounds back to v, so the decay is lost and only the 0.001·g² term can move v. The downward case stays at exactly 1.0. The upward case climbs one bf16 step at a time to 2.0 by step 200 and stops there, because at v = 2 the term 0.001·4 = 0.004 is below half a bf16 spacing (2⁻⁷ ≈ 0.0078).

1.title: On a 200-item slice, no net change below 3 points can reach p < 0.05, and the threshold rises with D.
1.caption: Computed exactly. For each discordant count D, the curve takes the smallest split k/(D−k) with two-sided binomial p < 0.05 and converts it to a net change of (D − 2k)/200. 2.title: Shared suffix logits turn the DPO gradient into a push-down on chosen tokens.
2.caption: Left: in a tabular policy the pair only touches $z_b$ and $z_c$, so $p(b|a)$, and with it chosen, can only rise. Right: in a network the suffix after $b$ and after $c$ maps to almost the same hidden state, so both pushes land on one logit $z_t$. The net push $p_l - p_w$ is negative whenever the model is less confident after its mistake. That lowers $\log\pi_\theta(y_w|x)$ even as the margin grows.

The include-self variance is lower only because that gradient is 7/8 as long (mean 0.0614 against the true 0.0700).

4.title: Week-0 train prompts mostly have 0 or 16 passes out of 16, so most G=8 groups carry no signal
4.caption: Real data from `runs/week0_sftpool_train_qwen3-1_7b/scored.jsonl`: the number of the 274 train prompts with c basic-test passes out of 16 samples (T=0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20). A random group of 8 has zero variance with probability 1 at c = 0 or 16, 0.5 at c = 1 or 15, 0.23 at c = 2 or 14, 0.1 at c = 3 or 13, and under 0.04 for 4 ≤ c ≤ 12. Averaged over prompts, that gives 36.1% all-fail and 43.6% all-pass groups.

6.title: GRPO spreads a fixed penalty over a wrong answer's length; Dr. GRPO gives every token the same weight.
6.caption: This is group 1 of `test_token_weights`: rewards (1, 0, 0), lengths (2, 4, 6), G=3, L_max=8. The loss averages over all 6 sequences in the test batch (two groups of 3), which is where the 6 in both denominators comes from. Each cell is a token position. Bar height is the gradient weight w on that token's log-prob (green pushes up, red pushes down). Dashed cells are padding and get zero gradient. Bar heights are scaled separately in each panel. Under GRPO the 6-token failure gets two-thirds of the per-token push of the 4-token one. Under Dr. GRPO both get the same per-token push, so the longer failure carries 1.5x the total penalty.

7.title: The rollout process never forks; each tool call runs in a fresh, namespaced, capped interpreter, and the checker runs elsewhere afterwards.

The final code reaches the hidden-test checker only after the episode, in a separate process.

7.title: Re-prefill FLOPs grow superlinearly with turns; the ratio to prefilling once is about (K+1)/2.
7.caption: Computed from $F(T) = 3.44\times10^9\,T + 114\,688\,T^2$ with an increment of 600 tokens per turn, so turn $k$'s context is $600k$. Re-prefill sums $F(600k)$ for $k = 1..K$. Prefill-once is $F(600K)$. At $K = 3$ the values are 13.0 vs 6.6 TFLOP, a ratio of 1.97. At $K = 10$ the ratio is 5.2, slightly below 5.5 because the quadratic term is a larger share of prefill-once.

The gap is the difference between averaging the formula over prompts and plugging in the average pass rate.

8.after: Length normalization when episodes span turns
8.title: Per-episode mean normalization gives short episodes 4x the per-token weight; constant and token-level normalization treat every token alike.
8.caption: Per-token gradient weight (in units of $10^{-3}$) for a batch of B = 4 episodes, computed from the section-7 formulas: per-episode mean $A_i/(B L_i)$, constant $A_i/C$ with $C = 1536 B$, and token-level $A_i/\sum_j L_j$ with $\sum_j L_j = 1000$. The episodes have L = 100 or 400 model tokens and A = ±1. This is arithmetic on a toy batch, not a measurement. Under the per-episode mean, being wrong at length costs a quarter as much per token as being wrong briefly.

9.after: Communication: ring all-reduce and the FSDP bill
9.title: Ring reduce-scatter on 4 devices: each step moves one chunk per device
9.caption: Each device's buffer is split into n = 4 chunks. At every step each device sends its outlined chunk to its right-hand neighbor, which adds it to its own copy (D3's send wraps around to D0 and is not drawn as an arrow). After n - 1 = 3 steps every device owns one fully reduced chunk (marked 'all') and has sent 3 chunks of P/4. An all-gather then circulates those reduced chunks for another 3 steps.

10.title: At d = 2048, almost every labeling of up to about 3,900 points is linearly separable, so a 400-item probe can memorize anything.
10.caption: Cover's function counting theorem, computed exactly: the fraction of the $2^N$ labelings of $N$ points in general position in $\mathbb{R}^d$ that a linear classifier with bias can realize is $P(\mathrm{Binom}(N-1, 1/2) \le d)$. The x axis is $N/(d+1)$, and every curve crosses 0.5 at 2. The transition gets sharper as $d$ grows. The left vertical line marks the section's random-label run, $N=400$ at $d=2048$ ($N/(d+1)=0.195$), well inside the region where train accuracy is always 100%.

10.title: With 50 random directions, no single layer can pass Holm across 28 layers; one confirmatory test can.
10.caption: Computed: the smallest empirical p-value that $K$ null directions can give is $1/(K+1)$. The first Holm threshold for $m=28$ layers is $0.05/28 = 0.0018$, which needs $K \ge 559$. A single pre-registered test on the report split only needs $p \le 0.05$, and $K=50$ (minimum $p = 0.020$) is enough for that.

10.after: Where training changed the weights: LoRA delta norms
10.title: Norms and singular values of a LoRA delta come from 16x16 cores, never from the full matrix.
10.caption: The `down_proj` delta $\Delta W$ is drawn to scale; the rank-16 factors are drawn thicker than scale so they stay visible. Forming the $2048 \times 6144$ product costs about 100 times more than the two Gram matrices whose trace product gives $\lVert BA \rVert_F^2$ (201M against 2.1M multiply-adds), and both Gram matrices use $A$ as well as $B$. The thin QR factors have orthonormal columns, so the singular values of $BA$ are those of the $16 \times 16$ core $R_B R_A^\top$. In qwix layout, $A$ = `lora_a`ᵀ and $B$ = `lora_b`ᵀ. Multiply by $s = 2$ at the end.

11.title: Speculative decoding helps only when acceptance is high and k is small. With overhead-heavy drafts it is a net loss.
11.caption: Modeled speedup $= \frac{1-\alpha^{k+1}}{1-\alpha} / (1 + k c)$ with draft cost $c$ in target steps. Solid lines use the bandwidth-only $c = 1.2/3.44 = 0.35$. The dashed line uses $c = 0.5$ (a draft dominated by per-layer overhead). Below 1.0 is a net loss. This is computed from the formula, not measured. Measure $\alpha$ from your own acceptance logs.

The batch limit is where the dashed reserve line crosses each pool line, so `max_batch` gives 60 at fraction 0.75 and 86 at 0.90. These are predictions, not profiler measurements.

12.title: Holm rejects only the first of nine comparisons, where five pass uncorrected
12.caption: The section's worked example on a log scale. Holm walks right from rank 1 and stops at the first p-value above its threshold (rank 2: 0.011 > 0.00625). Five p-values fall below the uncorrected 0.05 line. Holm's thresholds rise toward 0.05, so it is never less powerful than flat Bonferroni.

12.after: Too many comparisons: Holm and the two-level bootstrap
12.title: Seeds are resampled separately in each arm, items once for both arms
12.caption: One bootstrap replicate of `two_level_paired`. Seeds are separate training runs and are not paired across arms, so each arm draws its own seed rows. Item IDs are shared by both arms, so one item draw indexes both matrices and keeps the pairing. The histogram is schematic. The CI is its 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles. With 200 replicates the smallest possible p (0.01) can never pass Holm's first threshold.

13.title: Zeroing Adam's moments at step 141 makes updates almost 4x larger, and they stay large for many steps.
13.caption: Numpy simulation, not a training run: 20,000 coordinates with gradient mean 0.2 and noise SD 1, Adam with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, and a resume at step 141. The y-axis is the update RMS per coordinate, √mean(u²). Zeroing m and v but keeping the count gives 1.15 at the resume and still 0.85 twelve steps later. A full re-init (count = 0) gives exactly 1.0, which falls back to 0.34 within 12 steps. With a correct resume the update stays at 0.30.

13.title: Only the second step after a restore can detect lost optimizer state.
13.caption: The loss at step k is computed before that step's update, so it depends only on the restored params θ_k, and assert 1 passes in both lanes. Optimizer state first affects a loss at step k+1, through the update that produced θ_k+1. That is why the test in this section checks two steps, and why a second test should confirm that skipping `nnx.update(o2, got["opt"])` makes assert 2 fail.

13.after: The two-level paired bootstrap, and what five seeds cannot do
13.title: MBPP test is bimodal: 43% of items never pass and 35% always pass.
13.caption: Real data: `runs/week0_noise_test_qwen3-1_7b_s{0,1,2}/scored.jsonl`, Qwen3-1.7B base, 500 MBPP test items, 4 samples per item per seed pooled to 12, basic tests. Each bar is the percentage of items with that many passes out of 12. Because the item pass rates are piled at 0 and 1 (SD 0.46 across items), an unpaired arm mean carries about 2.1 pts of item noise. Pairing over items cancels these always-pass and never-pass items.

13.after: Predict the CI width and the MDE before you look
13.title: More seeds shrink the CI only down to the item floor, and the MDE never drops below 3.1 pts on 500 items.
13.caption: Computed from SE = √(2σ_s²/S + σ_d²/I) with σ_s = 2 pts, σ_d = 0.25 and I = 500. Half-width = 1.96·SE and MDE = 2.8·SE (80% power, two-sided 5%). Dashed lines are the limits as S grows without bound, where only the item term is left (2.19 and 3.13 pts). The 5-seed design sits at 3.3 and 4.7 pts. Normal quantiles are used, so at small S the true values are somewhat larger (see the t correction in section 4).

The dashed red block shows the 5.0 GB that full fp32 logits for an 8 × 1024 microbatch would add without chunking. Even the worst case (about 26 GB) stays under 32 GB on paper, but with little margin for XLA buffers, so free or donate the KV cache before the train step and chunk the log-probs. These are estimates; check them with `memory_analysis()` before renting.
